verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed every hidden case, so there were no functional failures to attribute to documentation gaps. The docs did well in the exact places this task needed: HTML Processor > Supported elements explains that WP_HTML_Processor is the structural choice for containment, depth, implied/virtual closers, and subtree walking; Overview > Recipe: scan a region before editing its opener gives the bookmark, forward scan, clean-scan check, seek-back, edit pattern; Overview > Recipe: test subtree membership and direct children states the direct-child opener checks using #tag, !is_tag_closer(), and parent depth + 1; next_tag() clarifies that tag_name is not a list of alternatives and shows scanning any tag then branching on get_tag(); get_current_depth() explains why subtree walks use >= and why child closers report the parent depth; next_token() and get_current_depth() both point callers to paused_at_incomplete_token() and get_last_error() for truncation/unsupported markup; set_attribute() documents overwriting/encoding semantics; get_updated_html() documents retrieving queued mutations while preserving untouched bytes. Near misses: trial-3 skipped the explicit #tag guard from the direct-child recipe, suggesting that examples which check only get_tag() can dilute that rule. Also, get_updated_html() and paused_at_incomplete_token() are inherited from WP_HTML_Tag_Processor and not first-class method headings in the HTML Processor page, so subjects had to connect the inheritance/cross-reference dots. Finally, the docs imply but could state more directly that clean-scan checks should apply to the region the caller actually scanned; trailing incomplete or unsupported markup after a closed region should not be discovered by over-scanning unless the caller's contract requires whole-document completeness.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all 7 hidden cases. The docs successfully led every subject to the key contract: the input is a BODY-context fragment, WP_HTML_Processor is the structural processor for normalized output, normalize() normalizes a BODY fragment, and normalize() returns string|null with null meaning unable to normalize. The HTML Processor overview and Supported elements section were especially useful because they say the HTML Processor should be chosen for normalizing markup, that unsupported markup aborts processing, and that output-producing methods such as serialize() and normalize() return null. The normalize() section also directly covered the tested transformations: quoted attributes, added omitted tags, lower-casing, re-encoding, and omitted incomplete trailing syntax. Near-miss: unsupported cases recorded E_USER_WARNING from WP_HTML_Processor::serialize even though the candidates only called normalize(). This did not break the functional contract here, but the rendered normalize() docs only state that null is returned if unable to normalize; they do not make warning side effects visible.

doc_gaps.problem: The return contract says null is returned if unable to normalize, but it does not state whether unsupported markup also emits a warning through the underlying serialize() path.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Document the observable side effects for unsupported input: either explicitly say normalize() may trigger the same E_USER_WARNING as serialize() before returning null, or guarantee and document warning-free null behavior if that is the intended API.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs imply normalize() is the shortcut for BODY-fragment normalization, but the relationship to create_fragment($html)->serialize() is only indirect.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add one sentence that normalize($html) is the convenience form for creating a BODY-context fragment processor and serializing it, so callers know when to use normalize() versus create_fragment()/serialize().

doc_gaps.problem: The section says output methods return null on unsupported markup, but does not distinguish parse failure from incomplete trailing syntax, which normalize() omits rather than treating as unsupported.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a small contract note contrasting unsupported parser aborts, which produce null, with incomplete trailing syntax, which is omitted from normalized serialization unless the caller separately requires complete-source validation.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden cases failed in any trial: all three passed 10/10 and produced no `_doing_it_wrong` records. trials.notes: Correctly used WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment for body-fragment, tree-aware text extraction. Every API call is documented: create_fragment, next_token, get_token_name, is_tag_closer, get_attribute, get_current_depth, get_token_type, get_modifiable_text. The depth-bounded #text walk is the documented pattern and handles decoded href/text, valueless href via is_string(), empty href, and unclosed anchors. Minor near-miss: it uses a nested token loop despite the docs warning that repeated regions can be easier to get wrong with nested cursor walks, though this shape matches the reference and passed cleanly.

Correct processor choice and no undocumented methods: create_fragment, next_token, get_token_type, get_tag, is_tag_closer, get_attribute, get_modifiable_text, get_last_error all appear in the rendered docs. The single-pass state machine follows the documented closer-driven pattern and handles attribute true/null/string semantics and decoded text. Near-misses: returning an empty array on any later get_last_error() is an all-or-nothing read policy that can discard links already parsed before unsupported markup, while the docs leave read-only extraction policy to the caller; also, a stack flushed on closers would output nested A records inner-before-outer if nested anchors were encountered.

Correctly chose WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment and used only documented methods. It applies the key edge rules: is_string() excludes missing and boolean href while preserving empty-string href, get_modifiable_text() is read only for #text tokens, and virtual closers make the unclosed-link case pass. The main weakness is the single $current record: it relies on A closers rather than a depth-bounded subtree walk or stack, and it clears current when any non-string A opener is seen. That is fine for the frozen cases but less robust around nested or foreign-content A elements.

verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 8 frozen cases: simple, no-href-excluded, entity-in-href-decoded, valueless-href, image-link-empty-text, entities-in-text, no-links, and unclosed-link. The docs worked well because they directly surfaced the needed concepts: the Tag Processor "Which processor should I use?" section says to use the HTML Processor for text content and subtree walking; the HTML Processor "Recipe: collect DOM-style text from a subtree" gives the #text-only pattern; get_attribute documents string|true|null semantics and decoded attribute values; get_modifiable_text documents decoded #text and warns not to treat all modifiable text as DOM text; next_token/get_current_depth explain virtual closers and the >= depth boundary that make unclosed anchors work. The near-misses were not hidden-test failures: trial-2 chose an all-or-nothing get_last_error policy that differs from the reference's best-effort prefix behavior on unsupported markup after a parsed link, and trials 2/3 would be shaky if nested A tokens appear in foreign or invalid markup because their closer-driven state is not explicitly ordered by opener document position.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial: all three passed 7/7. The docs did well at steering subjects to WP_HTML_Processor for structure, documenting create_fragment(), next_token()/next_tag(), virtual closers, add_class(), and get_updated_html() byte preservation. The main near-miss is that two successful trials still built their own list stack instead of using get_breadcrumbs(), which shows the docs explain the capability but do not make the common 'has any ancestor of these names' idiom obvious enough. Another near-miss is completion policy: trial 1 would return queued edits after an unsupported-parser abort, while trials 2 and 3 discard all edits on get_last_error(); the docs do not clearly state the recommended get_updated_html() policy after an HTML Processor scan aborts.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs explain breadcrumb paths and direct breadcrumb queries, but not the common operation 'does the current element have any ancestor matching X'.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short idiom showing array_slice( get_breadcrumbs(), 0, -1 ) to exclude the current element, then in_array() checks for ancestor membership.

doc_gaps.problem: Manual state loops are documented, but the docs do not clearly distinguish when a caller should prefer parser-owned ancestry over maintaining a parallel stack.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add guidance that get_breadcrumbs() or get_current_depth() should be preferred for current-token ancestry; manual stacks are for derived state not already represented by the parser.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs say serialize() and normalize() return null after unsupported markup, but do not define what queued attribute/class edits plus get_updated_html() mean after an abort.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Document that a scan abort may mean only a prefix was inspected, and give a recommended whole-document mutation policy: check get_last_error() before returning edits, or explicitly document partial-prefix behavior.

doc_gaps.problem: Inherited methods needed for mutation completion, especially get_updated_html() and paused_at_incomplete_token(), are easy to miss on the HTML Processor page.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add an inherited-methods subsection or mutation checklist linking get_updated_html(), get_last_error(), and paused_at_incomplete_token() together for class/attribute-edit workflows.

trials.notes: Used `WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment()` for browser-like fragment parsing, then a single `next_token()` depth-bounded walk from the first `TABLE`. All HTML API methods used are documented in the rendered files. The implementation follows the documented repeated-region/state-machine pattern, reads ordinary DOM text only from `#text` tokens via `get_modifiable_text()`, and relies correctly on virtual closers for omitted tags.

Correct processor choice and fully documented API usage. The single token loop, depth break, row/cell state, closer-driven flushes, and `#text`-only text accumulation match the docs' guidance. The extra `class_exists()` guard is unnecessary but not an HTML API hallucination or misuse.

Correctly uses the HTML Processor rather than the Tag Processor, with only documented methods. The depth-bounded `next_token()` loop and state variables are idiomatic for repeated structural extraction. It handles decoded entity text through `get_modifiable_text()` and omitted closers through the processor's virtual closing tokens.

verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 8 frozen cases, so there are no failed hidden cases to diagnose. The rendered docs did well in the areas this task stresses: the processor-selection guidance explicitly says to use `WP_HTML_Processor` when structure, text content, or implied/missing closing tags matter; `next_token()` documents virtual closers, inserted table structure such as synthesized `TBODY`, and the single-cursor hazard of nested loops; `get_current_depth()` explains the `>=` subtree boundary; and the DOM-style text recipe says to accumulate only `#text` tokens and use `get_modifiable_text()` for already-decoded text. The main near-miss is that candidates had to generalize from `LI`/`DT` examples to a two-level repeated extraction shape: rows containing cells. They all did that correctly here, but the docs could make that pattern more explicit without embedding this task's solution.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs show a one-level repeated extraction example (`DT` terms), but tasks often require nested repeated records where an outer item contains inner items. Subjects succeeded, but they had to infer how to manage two state variables and two closer-driven flush points.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a general nested repeated-region recipe using neutral placeholder element names, showing one token loop, an outer accumulator, an inner accumulator, child flush on child closer, and parent flush on parent closer. Note that implicit and end-of-input closers drive the same flush path.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs mention synthesized table structure and virtual tokens, but they do not explicitly connect that to token dispatch APIs like `get_token_name()`, `get_tag()`, and `is_tag_closer()` for inserted elements.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add one sentence that inserted/virtual elements are visited as ordinary current tokens for inspection APIs, while source-position features such as bookmarks may not be available for inserted tokens. Cross-link to the bookmark limitation.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs correctly explain decoded `#text` extraction and completion policy, but the read-only extraction examples do not show a concrete policy branch for incomplete input or unsupported-parser aborts.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short optional completion-policy snippet after the extraction recipe: after a bounded walk, check `paused_at_incomplete_token()` and `get_last_error()` when the caller requires complete-source results; otherwise document that returning accumulated browser-like text is an explicit caller policy.

trials.notes: Correctly used WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment(), next_token(), get_token_type(), get_modifiable_text(), and serialize_token() for a token-by-token normalized rewrite. All called HTML API methods are documented in the rendered files and execution recorded no _doing_it_wrong notices. Minor reservation: the create_fragment() fallback can return raw input via normalize($html) ?? $html, which would not preserve the normalized-output contract if both failed, though this path was not exercised.

Correct processor and main loop: HTML Processor fragment parsing, #text guard, decoded comparison via get_modifiable_text(), and wrapper output around serialize_token(). get_last_error() is documented and there were no _doing_it_wrong notices. The post-loop unsupported-markup fallback discards any emitted wrapper output by restarting from normalize($html), and then may return raw input if normalization fails, so its failure policy is less clean than the main documented rewrite pattern.

Correctly followed the documented serialize_token() rewrite pattern with WP_HTML_Processor, next_token(), #text checks, decoded get_modifiable_text(), and normalized token serialization. All HTML API methods used are present in the docs and execution showed no misuse notices. Minor reservation is the same raw-input fallback on processor-creation failure; the empty-keyword guard is harmless because the task specifies a non-empty keyword.

verdict.failure_analysis: No failed hidden/frozen cases occurred: all three trials passed all 8 cases. The docs did well on the central hazards for this task: they clearly steer normalized fragment work to WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment(), explain that next_token() visits ordinary #text tokens and virtual closers, state that get_modifiable_text() returns decoded text and is too broad unless guarded by get_token_type() === '#text', and provide a serialize_token() wrapper-rewrite example that is almost exactly the needed pattern. The near-miss across trials was fallback policy: candidates either ignored get_last_error() after the rewrite loop or used normalize($html) ?? $html as a fallback, which can discard emitted changes and may return non-normalized raw input. That did not affect the supported test cases, but it shows the docs could make rewrite failure policies more explicit.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs say create_fragment() can return null and normalize() can return null, but they do not strongly discourage raw-input fallback for functions whose contract promises normalized HTML.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short note: if the caller promises normalized or rewritten output, returning the original input is a distinct fallback policy and is not normalized; prefer an explicit sentinel, empty output, exception, or documented best-effort policy.

doc_gaps.problem: The page warns that normalize($html) after a rewrite discards emitted changes, but the complete post-loop failure-handling shape is easy to miss.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a compact generic rewrite skeleton showing: create processor, build $output with serialize_token(), then separately handle get_last_error() and optionally paused_at_incomplete_token() according to the caller's contract.

doc_gaps.location: html-processor.md, next_token() returns / loop completion discussion
doc_gaps.problem: A false next_token() result can mean normal completion, unsupported parser abort, or paused incomplete trailing syntax; the distinction is spread across several sections.
doc_gaps.suggestion: In next_token() or immediately after its examples, add a small table mapping loop-end conditions to checks: get_last_error() for unsupported markup, paused_at_incomplete_token() for truncated syntax, otherwise normal end.

trials.notes: Passed 6/6 frozen cases. All API methods used are documented. Main penalty: it used WP_HTML_Processor, and even tried create_full_parser() before create_fragment(), for a flat source-order class edit where the docs recommend WP_HTML_Tag_Processor. It did use bookmarks and get_updated_html() correctly, but next_token() was more complex than needed and it never checked get_last_error() or paused_at_incomplete_token() before trusting an end-to-end scan for the last H2.

Passed 6/6 frozen cases. All API methods used are documented. The traversal is cleaner than trial-1: next_tag(), repeated bookmark, seek(), add_class(), release_bookmark(), and get_updated_html(). The main issue is processor choice: WP_HTML_Processor is unnecessary and less robust for a flat tag/class edit. Its get_last_error()/paused_at_incomplete_token() guard is documented and cautious, but it can over-reject inputs that the Tag Processor could still edit byte-preservingly.

Passed 6/6 frozen cases. This closely matches the documented and canonical pattern: construct WP_HTML_Tag_Processor directly, scan H2 tags with next_tag(), keep one literal bookmark updated to the latest match, seek back, add_class(), release the bookmark, and return get_updated_html(). Minor deductions only for not checking set_bookmark()/seek failure beyond the final seek branch and not making an explicit incomplete-input policy.

verdict.failure_analysis:
All trials passed every frozen case, so there are no failed hidden cases to attribute. The docs worked well for this task in several places: the Tag Processor overview explicitly says to use it for flat, position-based tag/class edits; next_tag() documents string and array tag-name queries; add_class() documents creating/appending the class while preserving existing classes; get_updated_html() is clearly presented as the correct output API for queued edits; and the Tag Processor set_bookmark() section directly explains the general pattern of re-setting one bookmark on each match and seeking to it after the scan.

The near-misses were concentrated around processor selection. Trials 1 and 2 both chose WP_HTML_Processor despite explaining a flat tag edit. That choice passed the simple cases but inherits HTML Processor abort behavior on unsupported markup, which can make a 'last matching tag' scan incomplete. Trial 1 in particular did not check get_last_error() after a whole-input scan; on unsupported markup after an earlier H2 it could treat the last successfully visited H2 as the global last H2. Trial 2 did check parser error and incomplete-token state, which follows the HTML Processor safety guidance, but that same choice means it may return the original HTML in cases where the Tag Processor could safely mark the last source-order H2. These are not frozen-test failures, but they show that the docs still leave room for models to overuse the tree-aware processor for byte-preserving flat edits.

doc_gaps.location: WP_HTML_Processor overview / Which processor should I use?
doc_gaps.problem: The docs say the lighter Tag Processor suffices for flat attribute and class edits, but two subjects still selected the HTML Processor for a source-order 'last matching tag' edit.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short decision note: if the match is based only on source-order tag name, class, or attributes, prefer WP_HTML_Tag_Processor plus next_tag(); reserve WP_HTML_Processor for matches depending on DOM structure, subtree boundaries, implied tags, text extraction, or normalization.

doc_gaps.problem: The Tag Processor docs clearly mention re-setting one bookmark to remember the last match, but the HTML Processor's rendered set_bookmark() section is less explicit about re-setting an existing bookmark name moving it.
doc_gaps.suggestion: State in both rendered method docs that calling set_bookmark() again with the same literal name moves that bookmark to the current token, which is the intended bounded-memory pattern for remembering the latest match in a scan.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn that unsupported markup aborts the HTML Processor, but they do not make the consequence vivid for scans whose answer depends on reaching the end, such as last-match, count-all, or collect-all operations.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add guidance that any HTML Processor scan whose result depends on seeing the entire remaining input must treat non-null get_last_error() as an incomplete result before seeking back or mutating based on what was found so far.

doc_gaps.problem: For functions accepting either complete documents or fragments, subjects guessed factory order instead of recognizing that a flat byte-preserving edit avoids the factory choice entirely.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add factory-choice guidance saying that document-vs-fragment ambiguity is a reason to use WP_HTML_Tag_Processor when tree semantics are not required; when tree semantics are required, callers should choose the factory from their input contract rather than silently trying both as a default pattern.

doc_gaps.problem: The incomplete-token docs explain how scanning pauses, but do not clearly state the policy implications for earlier complete matches and queued edits. This can lead either to ignoring truncation when completeness matters or over-rejecting when the requested edit only touches an earlier complete token.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Clarify that earlier complete tokens and bookmarks remain editable after a pause, and advise callers to choose explicitly between best-effort byte-preserving updates and returning the original input when their result requires a complete scan.

trials.notes: Correctly chose WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for a flat attribute-removal task. All HTML API calls are documented: constructor usage, next_tag(), get_attribute_names_with_prefix(), remove_attribute(), and get_updated_html(). The loop is idiomatic and handles the documented null return from the prefix helper.

Same correct Tag Processor pattern as the reference. The response explicitly relied on documented case-insensitive prefix matching and lowercase returned names. No _doing_it_wrong records and no undocumented HTML API usage.

Correct documented API usage. The class_exists() guard is unnecessary in the harness but is a PHP builtin rather than a hallucinated HTML API method, and it does not affect the tested WordPress environment. The actual processor loop is idiomatic.

verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 7 frozen cases, so there are no failed hidden cases to attribute to misconceptions. The rendered docs did well in three places: the processor-choice guidance says to use the Tag Processor for flat attribute and class edits where byte-exact preservation matters; the usage section shows the constructor plus next_tag() plus mutation pattern; and get_attribute_names_with_prefix() states that matching is case-insensitive and returns lowercase names. The next_tag() docs also explain that tag-like text in comments/raw text is not matched and incomplete trailing tags are not modified, which supports the comment and malformed-input edge behavior. Near-misses: remove_attribute() itself is terse, and the empty-array case for get_attribute_names_with_prefix() is implied by behavior rather than explicitly documented in its return text.

doc_gaps.problem: The return contract says array|null but does not explicitly distinguish an empty array on a matched tag with no matching attributes from null when no tag opener is matched.
doc_gaps.suggestion: State that while matched on a tag opener the method returns an array of lowercase matching attribute names, possibly empty; it returns null only when the processor is not matched on a tag opener.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs say returned names are lowercase, but do not explicitly say those normalized names are safe to pass to attribute mutation methods.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a sentence that returned lowercase names may be passed directly to get_attribute(), set_attribute(), or remove_attribute(), since attribute-name matching is ASCII case-insensitive.

doc_gaps.problem: The method section does not repeat key removal semantics: ASCII case-insensitive lookup, no-op behavior for absent attributes or non-opener tokens, and preservation of surrounding source bytes.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Expand the docblock to state that lookup is ASCII case-insensitive, absent attributes are a no-op returning false, and removal deletes only the attribute token span while leaving neighboring whitespace and all untouched bytes unchanged.

trials.notes: Correctly used WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment(), a single next_token() walk, get_token_type()/get_tag() to identify SPAN tag tokens, and serialize_token() to build normalized rewritten output. All called methods are documented in the rendered files and no _doing_it_wrong records occurred. Minor issue: the raw-input fallback on create_fragment() failure or get_last_error() would not satisfy a normalized rewritten-output contract if reached.

Correct processor and documented API surface throughout, including documented WP_HTML_Processor::normalize(). The main loop is idiomatic and matches the serialize_token() rewrite pattern. The weakness is the fallback: normalize($html) after a token rewrite is specifically warned about because it restarts from the original bytes and would discard skipped SPAN tokens if that branch were reached.

Uses the intended HTML Processor fragment parser and the canonical token-serialization rewrite pattern. All methods are documented, and no misuse was reported. Minor edge-policy gap: it returns raw input if processor creation fails and never checks get_last_error(), so unsupported-parser aborts could produce a partial rewrite rather than an explicit fallback.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial: all three passed 7/7. The docs appear to have succeeded because the HTML Processor overview explicitly says to use it for structure and normalized output, create_fragment() matches body-fragment input, next_token() explains that walks see text plus opening and closing tokens including virtual closers, and serialize_token() directly documents the needed rewrite pattern: concatenate serialized tokens, skip tokens to remove them, and skip closers too. The serialize_token() section’s analogous SUP-removal example likely prevented the common mistakes of using get_updated_html(), using next_tag() without closers, or rebuilding text manually. Near-misses were limited to fallback semantics: candidates still wrote raw-input or normalize-original fallbacks, even though the docs warn those discard the accumulated rewrite. The unclosed-span case was handled because an unclosed element is virtually closed and serialized; it is not the same as a truncated/incomplete syntax token.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn that raw input and normalize($html) discard a rewrite, but candidates still used those as fallbacks in string-returning rewrite functions.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short contract-oriented note: for functions promising normalized rewritten HTML, returning raw input or normalize($html) is not equivalent to returning the rewrite; choose accumulated best-effort output, null/empty failure, or another explicit documented policy.

doc_gaps.problem: The distinction between an unclosed element that receives a virtual closer and a truly incomplete trailing syntax token is easy to miss.
